Introduction:
Emerging evidence suggests that reproductive health factors in adolescence are associated with diabetes incidence in adulthood [ 1–3 ]. The onset of menarche, or the first menstrual cycle, indicates sexual maturation and is the first milestone in a woman’s reproductive history [ 4 ]. Epidemiologic data from high-income countries (HICs) show that younger age at menarche is associated with 1.5 times higher risk of diabetes incidence [ 5–10 ]. It is not clear whether these findings extend to women in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) who exhibit different reproductive and metabolic profiles. On average, women in LMICs experience a later age at onset of menarche [ 11–13 ] and are less likely to be obese than women in HICs. India, a country with a high diabetes burden [ 14 , 15 ] and historically lower levels of obesity, offers an informative setting to evaluate the relationship between age at menarche and diabetes in the LMIC context.

Although the mechanisms underlying the link between early onset of menarche and type 2 diabetes are unclear, women with earlier onset of menarche are known to experience pronounced post-menarche adipose tissue accumulation [ 16 ] resulting in increased body mass index (BMI) and waist circumference in adulthood [ 17 , 18 ], which are important risk factors for development of diabetes [ 19 ]. However, the causal direction of the obesity-menarche association remains unclear as girls with childhood obesity experience rapid pubertal progression [ 17 , 20–22 ]. Genes controlling both age at menarche and glucose regulation also offer a possible explanation for this association [ 23 ]. Further, early menarche is associated with high levels of sex hormones and low levels of sex hormone-binding globulin, which in turn reduce insulin secretion and elevate blood glucose levels. It is hypothesized that with these hormonal features women with early menarche are therefore at higher risk of diabetes independent of adiposity [ 24–27 ].

To investigate the relationship between age at menarche and diabetes in adulthood, we estimated the longitudinal association between age at menarche and incident diabetes in women in the Cardiometabolic Risk Reduction in South Asia (CARRS) cohort. We also investigated the effect modification of this association by adult adiposity as it is a potential putative factor in this association from previously published studies.
Methods:
### Participants

The CARRS study was established in 2010–12 as a multi-centric, community-based prospective study to identify risk factors for cardio-metabolic diseases among South Asians. The details of the CARRS study have been described elsewhere [ 28 , 29 ] and the cohort has maintained excellent retention at follow-up examinations [ 30 ]. Briefly, the cohort comprised of 12 271 adults aged ≥20 years from two cities in India (Chennai and Delhi) at baseline. Trained staff obtained informed consent and collected data using a standard validated questionnaire to record information on health-related behaviours and assessment of disease outcomes.

Of the original cohort at baseline, we excluded men ( n = 5868) and women with pre-existing diabetes ( n = 1543) (see Fig. 1 ). Of 4860 women free of known diabetes at baseline, we excluded 953 due to missing biomarker data to confirm diabetes status or missing age at menarche or age at menarche not within the range and subsequently another 144 due to missing other study covariate. Further, 109 women were lost to follow-up and censored from the analysis. For this analysis, the analytic cohort therefore comprised 3654 women who were diabetes-free at baseline and were followed until an incident diabetes event through 2021. While some statistical differences were observed (between women in the analytic sample and those excluded from the analysis) due to the large sample size, the standardized differences were <0.2 suggesting that these differences were unlikely to introduce bias in further analyses ( Supplementary Table S1 ).

The CARRS study was approved by the Institutional Review Boards of the Public Health Foundation of India (IRB00006658), Delhi; All India Institute of Medical Sciences (IEC/NP-17/07.09.09), Delhi and Madras Diabetes Research Foundation (MDRF/EC/EPI/2009/10), Chennai. Additionally, the study received approval from the Health Ministry Screening Committee of the Government of India.

### Exposure and outcome assessment

The exposure for this analysis was age at menarche, in years, or age at first menstrual period. It was ascertained at baseline based on self-report queried through a questionnaire. Given that there is no universally accepted definition for early menarche and there is no prior work from India, we considered age at menarche in years as a continuous measure. The outcome for this analysis was incident diabetes. Incident diabetes cases were defined as study participants who were diabetes‐free at baseline and who had fasting plasma glucose levels ≥126 mg/dl (≥7.0 mmol/l) or HbA1c levels ≥6.5% (≥48 mmol/mol), or self‐reported medical diagnosis with prescription of glucose lowering drugs at follow‐up examinations [ 29 , 31 ]. On each of the biennial follow-ups, blood samples were collected for assessment of diabetes status whereas, participants were asked about physician-diagnosed diabetes at each annual follow-up visit. The date of onset of diabetes was considered as the date of most recent follow-up visit after the diagnosis of diabetes.

### Covariates

Participants reported information on socio-demographics (age, monthly household income, education, marital status, religion, and ownership of assets), lifestyle factors [ever-use of tobacco/alcohol, work-related vigorous physical activity [ 32 ], fruit/vegetable consumption (modified food frequency questionnaire)], first-degree family history of diabetes, medical history or presence of a chronic condition (hypertension, heart disease, stroke, kidney disease, dyslipidaemia), and reproductive history (number of pregnancies, menopause status) at baseline.

Physical measurements (blood pressure, height, weight, waist circumference) were recorded using standardized procedures [28]. Those with measured waist circumference ≥80 cm were grouped as women with central obesity. We calculated the BMI as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared. Although, literature supports the use of waist circumference as a more useful obesity index in the Indian population to assess the risk of cardiometabolic conditions, we included both the measures in our analysis [ 33 ].

### Statistical analysis

We accounted for the complex survey design in the statistical analysis and all estimates apply survey weights.

We summarized the participant characteristics as prevalence [95% confidence interval (CI)] for categorical variables and mean [standard deviation (SD) and 95% CI] for continuous variables for the overall sample and compared the same by incident diabetes status. The difference in the age at menarche by participant characteristics was also computed using the adjusted Wald test.

We next calculated the incidence rate of diabetes (95% CI) by the age at onset of menarche. In the absence of definitive age categories for menarche in the Indian population, we empirically established groups based on the distribution of menarche timing and diabetes incidence within our cohort. To achieve this, we computed available sample sizes and the number of diabetes events across each year of age at menarche. Drawing on this tabulation, we categorized menarche timing into four groups: ≤12 years, 13 years, 14 years, and ≥15 years. In our further analysis, age at menarche was analysed both, as a continuous and a categorical exposure.

We calculated person years of follow-up as the number of years from baseline to first diagnosis of diabetes, death, loss of follow-up, or end of follow-up (2021) whichever came first. We performed Cox proportional hazards analyses to estimate the hazard ratio (HR) comparing the incidence of diabetes by menarche age. We evaluated the proportionality assumption through the Schoenfeld residual test, which indicated no significant violation of the assumption ( P -value = 0.109). Based on the hypothesized causal pathways drawing on prior literature, we sequentially included five sets of covariates in separate models. The unadjusted model was followed by addition of baseline age of women (in model 1). We next included other socio-demographic variables (city, education, wealth index, marital status, religion), and family history of diabetes (in model 2), and lifestyle factors (physical activity, tobacco use, fruit/vegetable consumption) and presence of a chronic condition (in model 3). The final set of models incorporated adiposity measures as potential mediating factors: waist circumference as a measure of central obesity (model 4a) and BMI as a measure of general obesity (model 4b).

We assessed statistical interaction between age at menarche and obesity (BMI and waist circumference classifications, separately) using the P -value of the Wald test and also conducted Cox proportional hazards analyses stratified by obesity classification.

Lastly, we conducted an analysis restricting to women aged 20–45 years at baseline. This analysis addressed the higher potential for recall bias in the age at menarche among older women and allowed us to explore associations of interest in an age group that reported a younger age at menarche on average.

All analysis was performed using the STATA statistical package (StataCorp. 2019. Stata Statistical Software: Release 16 .1 College Station, TX: StataCorp LLC.).
Results:
Table 1 shows the baseline characteristics of women. The mean age (SD) of 3654 women free of diabetes at enrolment was 37.7 (SD = 10.4; range: 20–85) years, 59.9% were from Chennai and 64.0% had high to secondary school education. More than 50% of women had waist circumference ≥80 cm and slightly over 70% had a BMI ≥23 kg/m 2 . Women who developed incident diabetes were, on average, older in age at baseline. A higher proportion of women residing in Delhi developed incident diabetes over follow-up. Additionally, women who developed incident diabetes were more likely to report menopause, had an existing chronic condition, a family history of diabetes and were obese at baseline.

The mean (SD) age at onset of menarche was 13.9 (SD = 1.3; range: 9–18) years in the total sample. Supplementary Table S2 shows mean age at menarche by demographic and health characteristics. Younger women (20–39 years: 13.7, 40–59 years: 140.0, and ≥60 years: 13.9 years; P <.001) and those having a family history of diabetes (13.7 vs 13.9 years; P = .001) had a significantly earlier age at onset of menarche compared to their counterparts. Although women with general and central obesity had an earlier onset of menarche compared to their counterparts, the difference was not significant.

The incidence rate of diabetes by groups of age at onset of menarche is shown in Table 2 . Over ∼11 years of follow-up (median: 9.2 years; range: 0.09–11.05 years), there were 390 incident diabetes cases. The overall incidence rate of diabetes was 12.4 per 1000 person-years (95% CI 11.23–13.69); cumulative incidence was 10.7% (95% CI 9.32–12.33). Diabetes incidence rate was highest among women with menarche onset at 13 years, 14.0 per 1000 person-years (95% CI 11.69–16.80).

Table 3 shows the Cox proportional hazards analysis of age at menarche with incident diabetes. We did not observe an association between age at onset of menarche in years (treated as a continuous measure) and incident diabetes in any of the models. The unadjusted association between age at menarche and incident diabetes was HR = 1.03 (95% CI 0.94–1.14). After adjusting for age, demographics, and other confounding factors ( Table 3 , model 4a), the HR was 1.04 (95% CI 0.95–1.14).

When menarche onset age was analysed as distinct categories ( Table 3 ), we found no significant associations between age at menarche and incident diabetes. After adjusting for age, demographics, and other confounding factors ( Table 3 , Model 3), compared to women who experienced menarche at age 12, women with age at menarche of 13 had HR = 1.26 (95% CI 0.80–2.01), those at age 14 had HR = 1.16 (95% CI 0.73–1.83), and those at age 15 or older had HR = 1.28 (95% CI 0.79–2.06). These HR estimates remained similar even when we accounted for central and general obesity measures (Models 4a and 4b).

Supplementary Table S3 shows models with continuous age at menarche stratified by waist circumference and BMI. The point estimates for the HR for the association between age at menarche in years and incident diabetes were consistently higher in women with waist circumference ≤80 cm vs >80 cm and in women with BMI ≥23 vs BMI <23, but none of these associations were statistically significant. Moreover, there was no evidence of statistical interaction between age at menarche with central obesity (Wald P = 0.145) or general obesity (Wald P = 0.138).

Sensitivity analyses restricted to women aged 20–45 years demonstrated that the incidence of diabetes was progressively lower for every one year later onset of menarche, HR = 0.97 (95% CI 0.88–1.07) (model 4a), though this was not a statistically significant finding ( Supplementary Table S4 ).
Discussion:
To our knowledge, this is the first prospective study of age at menarche and incident type 2 diabetes among women in India, a setting with rapidly rising diabetes in the last two decades [ 15 , 34 , 35 ]. Roughly one in 10 women aged 20–85 years newly developed diabetes over the 11 years of follow-up. On average, women in our cohort experienced menarche at 13.9 years, nearly one year later than the global average [ 5–7 , 18 ]. In contrast to findings in some populations [ 8 ], we did not find evidence of an association between age of onset menarche and incident type 2 diabetes in this setting. The null association remained unchanged after adjustment for and stratification by adiposity.

Although many studies have reported heightened risk of diabetes among women with earlier onset of menarche, the findings remain inconclusive, and associations appear to vary across race, ethnicity, and geography. The strongest and most consistent associations have been reported among white women and populations with an earlier average age of menarche [ 8 ]. While White women in the ARIC cohort had a higher risk of incident diabetes, no association was observed among African American women [ 7 ]. In a separate study of Chinese women, the risk of incident diabetes was higher among women those with an earlier onset of menarche, and the association was attenuated on adjustment for adult adiposity [ 36 ]. A recent analysis of the data from 262 368 women diabetes free at baseline in the UK Biobank cohort demonstrates that women with early menarche ( < 12 years) had a higher risk of incident diabetes (HR 1.08, 95% CI: 1.02–1.13) compared to women experiencing menarche at 13 years [ 3 ].

Beyond differences in racial and ethnic composition of study populations, the definition of early menarche varies, with some studies considering it as occurring before age 12, while others set the threshold at before 14 years. A meta-analysis of 14 studies found that women who experienced early menarche had a 22% higher risk of type 2 diabetes compared with women who did not experience early menarche [ 9 ]. A more recent meta-analysis of 28 studies reported very similar levels of excess risk (19% higher diabetes) in women with earlier onset of menarche [ 8 ]. In most of these studies, associations between menarche age and diabetes were attenuated after adjusting for adiposity [ 5 , 7 , 37 ]. Surprisingly, women in the earliest menarche group (≤12 years) in our study had the lowest incidence rate of diabetes, though the relative risk of diabetes was not statistically different between these women and women who experienced menarche at older ages.

While women in LMICs have historically reported later age at menarche onset than HIC counterparts [ 38 , 39 ], age at onset of menarche appears to be declining in the Indian population and globally [ 11 , 40 ]. Women in the 20–39 years age group in our cohort reported younger average age at menarche relative to the ≥40 year age group, providing additional evidence of earlier age of onset of menarche in more recent birth cohorts. Beyond genetic factors [ 41–43 ], earlier onset of menarche can be attributed to socio-economic development and the associated transition to more obesogenic lifestyles characterized by greater linear growth and relative weight gain in infancy and early childhood [ 44–52 ]. While it is understood that pubertal maturation is often preceded by rapid childhood growth and that girls with earlier onset of menarche tend to have higher BMIs [ 48 , 49 ], evidence also suggests that earlier onset of menarche can lead to post-menarche adiposity and insulin resistance, contributing to development of diabetes [ 20 , 53 , 54 ]. Given the ongoing nutritional and epidemiological transitions in India, the relationship between menarche onset and diabetes warrant additional research in younger women who are likely to experience differing environments from the CARRS cohort.

Primary strengths of this study include prospective data from large community-based representative sample of women with objective measures of glycaemic status to define diabetes over an 11 year follow up period. The key limitation of this study is the potential for recall bias in the self-reported age at menarche and the lack of information on health characteristics during childhood and adolescence such as BMI and lifestyle factors. Regarding recall bias, evidence suggests a high correlation between the menarche age assessed by recall during adulthood and that obtained prospectively in childhood [ 55 , 56 ]. Furthermore, our analyses restricted to younger women who would ostensibly be more likely to accurately recall age at menarche reinforced the findings in the full cohort. Regarding characteristics in childhood and adolescents, many of these factors are likely mediators which ought not to be adjusted for to derive unconfounded associations. We note that the differences in the characteristics of the analytic sample and the original cohort limit the potential generalizability of the findings to the population of urban women residing in the two study sites. We emphasize that the standardized difference in age at menarche is <0.1, suggesting sufficient covariate balance and therefore the potential for selection bias due to study inclusion criteria is low [ 57 ].

In summary, we did not observe an association between onset of menarche and risk of incident type 2 diabetes in a large population-based cohort of Indian women. Given the global trend towards earlier puberty timing, future longitudinal studies with younger populations and longer follow-up duration are warranted to further investigate the possible role of menarche timing in diabetes development.
